items.title: George Wein interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: Mrs. Chaloff... her son was Serge Chaloff, Serge went to school with me.

ctx.x: No, okay. But she could read the sheet music and so forth. Oh that’s great. So you kind of naturally, you had the piano in the house. Did anybody have to push you into it?

I studied classical piano when I was about seven or eight years old and I started. I played classical for about four or five years. I studied with a very famous teacher, but she wasn’t famous when I studied with her, Mrs. Chaloff and she later became Madame Chaloff at the Berklee College, and her son was Serge Chaloff, Serge went to school with me. And she was a wonderful woman, and she really gave me a technique. She didn’t teach me a lot about music, which was unfortunate, because that’s one of the reasons I…
Was there a point where the classical lessons just wasn’t enough?

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: There were other musicians a year ahead of me, some great musicians: Serge Chaloff and Hal McKusick... They left school as soon as they could and went on the road with Tommy Reynolds and bands like that.

ctx.x: Were you the only kid in your class or group of friends that had a band?

Oh yes. Nobody else had a band. There were other musicians a year ahead of me, some great musicians: Serge Chaloff and Hal McKusick, and they went out and they were much better musicians. But they didn't have their bands, they just had much more natural musical talent. This was a little later. This is when we were seventeen and they were eighteen. They left school as soon as they could and went on the road with Tommy Reynolds and bands like that. The war was
on then and so there was a need for young people to go with these dance bands that were still out there.
